[THOUGHT] The patient has recurrent purulent skin infections and regional lymphadenitis beginning in infancy, fever and leukocytosis with left shift, and a defective neutrophil oxidative burst with an abnormal NBT test. These findings are classic for a phagocyte respiratory-burst defect due to NADPH oxidase deficiency leading to impaired intracellular killing. Other entities (e.g., leukocyte adhesion deficiency) would show markedly different features (poor pus formation, delayed umbilical separation) and normal oxidative burst. Immunofluorescence mapping ruled out epidermolysis bullosa, making a primary blistering disorder unlikely. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is CGD from NADPH oxidase complex deficiency (most commonly X-linked gp91phox mutation unless genetic testing shows otherwise).

[THOUGHT] The key diagnostic test findings (abnormal nitroblue tetrazolium test and decreased neutrophil oxidative burst activity) are highly specific for a phagocyte NADPH oxidase defect such as chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). The clinical picture—recurrent purulent skin infections since infancy, regional lymphadenopathy, fever, and leukocytosis—is consistent with CGD manifestations (recurrent catalase-positive infections, skin/soft tissue abscesses, lymphadenitis). Immunofluorescence mapping was normal, making an inherited blistering disorder (epidermolysis bullosa) unlikely. Alternative diagnoses that could mimic this picture (e.g., leukocyte adhesion deficiency) are less consistent because LAD classically has poor pus formation and delayed wound healing; MPO deficiency typically has different laboratory signatures. 

Red flags / missing critical data: exact NBT/DHR quantitative results (percent positive cells / MFI) and whether testing was repeated to exclude technical error; organism culture results from purulent lesions; absolute neutrophil count; flow cytometric DHR assay to confirm and quantify residual activity; genetic testing for NADPH oxidase subunit mutations (e.g., CYBB) for definitive confirmation; routine histology result from biopsy. Despite these missing details, the abnormal NBT plus decreased oxidative burst in the setting of recurrent childhood pyogenic infections is sufficiently specific to support CGD as the single most likely diagnosis.

[DECISION] PASS
